bai.ten: Light cones around a black hole
bai.moTa: The cones tilt inward step by step; the horizon is a surface woven from light
bai.yChinh: The closer to a black hole, the more the light cones tilt inward. At the horizon, the outer edge of the cone stands vertical: even outgoing light just stays where it is. Inside, the whole cone points toward the center: the radius r plays the role of time, and the singularity is a moment that is sure to come, not a place that can be avoided.
bai.conSo.1: **(π/2)·rs/c**: the longest proper time anyone can live inside the horizon; for Sgr A* it is 67 seconds.
bai.conSo.2: **2/3·rs/c**: how long someone falling from far away takes to get from the horizon to the singularity; 28 seconds for Sgr A*, 66 microseconds for a black hole of 10 solar masses.
bai.conSo.3: **12 rs²/r⁶**: the Kretschmann curvature invariant; finite at the horizon, infinite at the center.
bai.conSo.4: **3.6 million g**: the acceleration needed to hover at 1.01 rs around Sgr A*.
bai.hieuDung: **Someone falling in is not “frozen” at the horizon.** The frozen picture is only what a distant observer sees, because light emitted near the horizon arrives later and later without limit. By their own clock, the person falling in crosses the horizon and reaches the singularity in a finite time.
bai.nguon: Formulas: J. B. Hartle, Gravity (2003), ch. 12; Taylor, Wheeler and Bertschinger, Exploring Black Holes. Mass of Sgr A*: GRAVITY Collaboration (about 4.3 million solar masses). Mass of M87*: Event Horizon Telescope 2019, ApJL 875, L1 (6.5 billion). Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012. All other numbers are computed in code and checked in kiem-tra/kiem-non-lo-den.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Read a spacetime diagram of a black hole: the time axis, the horizon, the singularity, the light cones.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why the cones tilt inward step by step, and why outgoing light stands still at the horizon.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Say why every world line inside the horizon reaches r = 0, and calculate the proper time that remains.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Distinguish a coordinate singularity (r = rs) from a true singularity (r = 0) using a curvature invariant.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Calculate the real numbers for Sgr A*, M87* and a stellar-mass black hole.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: Far from the black hole: cones at almost 45°
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
This is a {{sơ đồ không-thời gian|spacetime diagram}} around a black hole. The vertical axis is time; the floor is two-dimensional space around the black hole (with one dimension left out, as in Lesson 4). The black hole sits on the central axis: the **golden cylinder** is the {{chân trời sự kiện|event horizon}}, and the **red zigzag line** is the {{kỳ dị|singularity}}.

Each funnel is the future {{nón ánh sáng|light cone}} of an event, as in Lesson 5: every world line leaving the tip of a cone must stay inside it. Look at the row of cones on the left, from the outside in. At the outer edge of the floor ($r = 6\,r_s$) the cone stands almost upright: its inner edge is tilted at exactly 45°, its outer edge at 35.5°, only slightly different from a flat-spacetime cone. Spacetime there is nearly flat.

Units in this lesson: radius is measured in {{bán kính Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild radii}} $r_s$, time in $r_s/c$. For the black hole at the center of the Milky Way (Sgr A*), $r_s \approx 12{,}7$ million km and $r_s/c \approx 42$ seconds.

> [Thử ngay] Overlay the “flat” cones of Lesson 5 (white frames) on each cone to compare. At $6\,r_s$ they nearly coincide; closer to the black hole they clearly differ. Hover over a cone to read the tilt of its two edges.
> [[Overlay flat cones to compare|phang]] [[Remove flat cones|boPhang]] [[Side view|ngang]]

> [Lưu ý] The cones are drawn large so they are easy to see; strictly, a light cone only tells you the allowed **directions** at a single point. The floor draws $r$ and the angle $\varphi$ as on a flat sheet of paper, without the curvature of space (covered in Lesson 11).

+++ Going deeper: how far has the cone shifted at $6\,r_s$?
Step 3 gives the formula. Plugging in numbers in advance: at $r = 6\,r_s$ the inner edge is tilted at exactly 45° and the outer edge has $\dd r/\dd t^* = 5/7$, that is, a tilt of 35.5° from the time axis. At $r = 100\,r_s$ the outer edge is tilted at 44.4°: almost a flat-spacetime cone. The black hole only tilts the cones noticeably within a few tens of $r_s$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Hover over the cones in the two rows on the left and find the cone whose **outer edge is vertical**: an outgoing light ray there cannot move outward at all.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: A cone’s color tells you its region: yellow outside, white exactly at the horizon, orange-red inside. The legend shows dr/dt* for the outer edge.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Why we need a different way to measure time
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Earlier lessons measured time with the $t$ of the {{metric Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild metric}}: the clock of someone at rest **very far** from the black hole. With that clock, light traveling along the radius obeys

$$ \frac{c\,\dd t}{\dd r} = \pm \frac{r}{r - r_s} $$

Near the horizon the right-hand side goes to infinity: light seems to “stand still”, the cone closes into a thread, and someone falling in needs $t \to \infty$ to reach the horizon. With numbers: at $r = 1{,}1\,r_s$, $c\,\dd t/\dd r = 11$; at $1{,}01\,r_s$ it is already 101.

But the person falling in notices nothing strange: their own clock (proper time) ticks normally, and they cross the horizon after a finite time. What breaks down is **the clock chosen to set up the coordinates**, not spacetime itself.

The fix: define a new time tied to infalling light rays, the time of {{tọa độ Eddington–Finkelstein|Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates}}:

$$ t^* = t + \frac{r_s}{c}\ln\left|\frac{r}{r_s} - 1\right| $$

With $t^*$, every infalling light ray is a straight 45° line, even as it crosses the horizon.

> [Thử ngay] The light-ray map on the left half: yellow rays go “out”, white rays go “in”. Switch back and forth and watch them stand up vertically and then straighten out again at the horizon.
> [[Measure with Schwarzschild time|schw]] [[Measure with time t*|ef]]

+++ Going deeper: from the Schwarzschild metric to the Eddington–Finkelstein metric
Set $r_s = c = 1$ and drop the angular direction. The Schwarzschild metric: $\dd s^2 = -(1 - 1/r)\,\dd t^2 + \dd r^2/(1 - 1/r)$.

From $t = t^* - \ln|r - 1|$ we get $\dd t = \dd t^* - \dd r/(r - 1)$. Substitute and use $(1 - 1/r)/(r - 1) = 1/r$:

$$ \dd s^2 = -\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{r}\right)\dd t^{*2} + \tfrac{2}{r}\,\dd t^*\dd r $$

$$ \qquad + \left[\tfrac{r}{r-1} - \tfrac{1}{r(r-1)}\right]\dd r^2 $$

The square bracket equals $(r^2 - 1)/(r(r-1)) = 1 + 1/r$. So

$$ \dd s^2 = -\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{r}\right)\dd t^{*2} + \tfrac{2}{r}\,\dd t^*\dd r $$

$$ \qquad + \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{r}\right)\dd r^2 + r^2\dd\varphi^2 $$

No coefficient is infinite at $r = 1$. Infalling light: try $\dd r = -\dd t^*$ and you get $-(1 - 1/r) - 2/r + 1 + 1/r = 0$ for every $r$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: Moving closer: the cones tilt inward
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
From now on we use $t^*$. The large cone at the top is the **probe cone**: drag the **Probe cone radius** slider below to bring it closer to the black hole.

The inner edge of the cone (infalling light) is always tilted at 45°. The outer edge (outgoing light) gradually stands up:

$$ \frac{\dd r}{\dd t^*} = c\,\frac{r - r_s}{r + r_s} $$

Here $r$ is the radius where the light is emitted and $r_s$ is the horizon radius. With numbers:

| $r$ | $\dd r/\dd t^*$ of the outgoing ray | Angle from the time axis |
|---|---|---|
| $6\,r_s$ | $0{,}71\,c$ | 35.5° |
| $3\,r_s$ | $0{,}50\,c$ | 26.6° |
| $2\,r_s$ | $0{,}33\,c$ | 18.4° |
| $1{,}25\,r_s$ | $0{,}11\,c$ | 6.3° |

So the whole cone leans toward the black hole. Outgoing light can still get out, but more and more slowly in terms of $t^*$. Anything with mass has to travel inside the cone, so it is slower still.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the yellow dot at the tip of the probe cone left and right along the radius and watch the outer edge stand up. Or press: [[Cone at 6 rs|r6]] [[At 3 rs|r3]] [[At 1.6 rs|r16]] [[At 1.25 rs|r125]]
> With sound on, a sustained note plays as the probe cone moves: its pitch follows the outward speed of the outer edge (converted for the ear: at the horizon it is the note A at 220 Hz, and every $0{,}5\,c$ faster raises it an octave, slower lowers it). A bell rings when the tip of the cone crosses the horizon.

> [Lưu ý] How much a cone tilts depends on how the time coordinate is chosen. What does not depend on it is **which directions can be reached and which cannot**: the edges of the cone are always made of exactly the light rays, as step 7 will show.

+++ Going deeper: why a slice of the cone is an off-center ellipse
Set $r_s = c = 1$. Take a small step of length $\dd t^* = \varepsilon$ in time, moving $\dd r$ along the radius and $\dd n = r\,\dd\varphi$ sideways. It lies on the cone when $\dd s^2 = 0$:

$$ \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{r}\right)\dd r^2 + \tfrac{2\varepsilon}{r}\dd r + \dd n^2 = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{r}\right)\varepsilon^2 $$

Multiply both sides by $r$ and complete the square:

$$ (r + 1)\left(\dd r + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{r + 1}\right)^2 + r\,\dd n^2 = \frac{\varepsilon^2 r^2}{r + 1} $$

That is an ellipse: its center is shifted inward by $\varepsilon/(r + 1)$, its radial semi-axis is $\varepsilon r/(r + 1)$, and its sideways semi-axis is $\varepsilon\sqrt{r/(r + 1)}$. The outer edge is at $\dd r = \varepsilon(r - 1)/(r + 1)$, the inner edge at $\dd r = -\varepsilon$. For $r = 3$: center shift $0{,}25\varepsilon$, semi-axes $0{,}75\varepsilon$ and $0{,}87\varepsilon$, outer edge $0{,}5\varepsilon$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the probe cone to where its outer edge is tilted at exactly **20°** from the time axis (within 1.5°).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: The label on the probe cone shows its tilt. From the table, it is 18.4° at 2 rs and 26.6° at 3 rs, so the spot you want is in between, closer to 2 rs.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: At the horizon: outgoing light stands still
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Bring the probe cone to exactly $r = r_s$. The outer edge of the cone **stands vertical**: $\dd r/\dd t^* = 0$. A flash of light emitted outward from exactly the horizon cannot move out at all; it stays at $r = r_s$ forever. The rest of the cone all points inward.

The vertical lines running up the golden cylinder are exactly such light rays. The horizon **is not a material surface**: there is no shell, no wall. It is a surface woven from light, the boundary between events that can still send a signal out and events that no longer can.

That is why someone falling through the horizon meets nothing special there. For a large black hole the tidal force there is still small: the difference in acceleration between the head and feet of a 2 m tall person is only about one ten-thousandth of $g$ at Sgr A*. But for a black hole of 10 solar masses, that figure is about 21 million $g$.

> [Thử ngay] [[Put the probe cone exactly at the horizon|r1]] [[Just outside: 1.05 rs|r105]] [[Just inside: 0.95 rs|r095]]
> Drag the tip of the probe cone back and forth across the horizon: the tip snaps slightly to the horizon circle so it is easy to place, and a bell rings every time it crosses.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “The horizon is where gravity suddenly becomes infinitely strong.” No. The curvature there is finite (step 7). What is infinite at the horizon is the cost of **staying still** there (step 8), because standing still at the horizon would require moving outward at the speed of light.

+++ Going deeper: the tidal force at the horizon
The radial difference in acceleration between two points a distance $L$ apart is $\Delta a \approx 2GM L/r^3$ (Lesson 12). At $r = r_s = 2GM/c^2$:

$$ \Delta a = \frac{c^2}{r_s^2}\,L $$

It is inversely proportional to the square of $r_s$, that is, to the square of the mass: the heavier the black hole, the “gentler” its horizon. Sgr A*: $r_s = 1{,}27 \times 10^{10}$ m, $\Delta a \approx 1{,}1 \times 10^{-3}$ m/s² for $L = 2$ m. A black hole of 10 solar masses: $r_s = 29{,}5$ km, $\Delta a \approx 2{,}1 \times 10^{8}$ m/s².
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the probe cone **inside** the horizon, to where even the outer edge already tilts **5° inward** (within 2°).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: Just inside the horizon the outer edge tilts inward only slightly; the deeper you go, the more it tilts. The spot you want is about 0.84 rs from the center. Scroll to zoom in; click the yellow dot and use the arrow keys to nudge it bit by bit.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Inside: every future leads to r = 0
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Bring the probe cone inside the horizon (an orange-red cone). Now **both edges** point toward the center: even the “outgoing” ray has $\dd r/\dd t^* \lt 0$. Every world line lies inside the cone, so every object, whichever way it fires its rockets, has $r$ decreasing. At $r = 0{,}6\,r_s$, even the “outgoing” ray falls inward with $\dd r/\dd t^* = -0{,}25\,c$.

Inside the horizon, $r$ plays the role of **time**: decreasing $r$ is like moving on to tomorrow, and nobody can stop it. So the singularity $r = 0$ is not a place ahead of you that you could steer around; it is **a moment** in the future of everyone who has gone inside.

The proper time left is finite. The longest possible is

$$ \tau_{\max} = \frac{\pi}{2}\,\frac{r_s}{c} $$

reached by falling freely from rest right at the horizon. Firing rockets only makes this time **shorter**: here the free-fall path is the one with the longest proper time, just like the twins in Lesson 6.

> [Thử ngay] [[Probe cone at 0.85 rs|r085]] [[At 0.6 rs|r06]] [[At 0.35 rs|r035]]
> Drag the probe cone deeper: the data box shows how much proper time someone falling from far away still has, as they pass that spot, before reaching the singularity.

+++ Going deeper: why the longest is π/2
Set $r_s = c = 1$. Inside, $1 - 1/r \lt 0$, so in the Schwarzschild metric the $\dd t^2$ term turns positive and the $\dd r^2$ term turns negative: $r$ is a timelike coordinate. For a freely falling object with specific energy $E$:

$$ \left(\frac{\dd r}{\dd\tau}\right)^2 = E^2 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{r}\right) \ge \frac{1}{r} - 1 $$

so $|\dd r/\dd\tau| \ge \sqrt{1/r - 1}$, and

$$ \tau \le \int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac{r}{1 - r}}\,\dd r = \frac{\pi}{2} $$

(substitute $r = \sin^2\theta$). Equality holds when $E = 0$: the object is at rest exactly at the horizon and then let go. Someone falling from far away has $E = 1$, so only $2/3$ is left.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Drag the probe cone to where someone falling freely from far away, as they pass that spot, has exactly **0.2 rs/c** of proper time left before reaching the singularity (within 0.03).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Someone falling from far away has $\tau = \tfrac{2}{3}\,(r/r_s)^{3/2}$ left (Summary tab, formula 4). Read the line “Faller from far away passing here” in the data box; scroll to zoom in so it is easier to place.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: The one who falls and the one who stays far away
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Move to the right half. The **pink line** is the world line of an astronaut falling freely from far away; at $t^* = 0$ they pass $r = 6\,r_s$. The white dots on the line mark every $r_s/c$ of proper time. Every $0{,}6\,r_s/c$ on their own clock, they send out a **flash of light** (yellow dot). The thick yellow stroke is the outgoing part of the light, the faint stroke the ingoing part. The vertical **blue line** is someone standing still at $r = 7\,r_s$.

- The first 16 flashes escape. The interval between two receptions, measured by the distant observer’s clock, keeps growing: 0.95; 0.96; 0.98; … ; 2.11; 4.23 $r_s/c$ (graph below).
- Flash 16, sent at $r \approx 1{,}13\,r_s$, is the **last** one to arrive. The closer to the horizon a flash is sent, the later it arrives, without limit.
- Flash 17 is sent at $r \approx 0{,}45\,r_s$, inside: both halves of it fall into the singularity.

The distant observer sees the astronaut’s image grow **slower, redder and fainter**, and never sees them cross the horizon. The astronaut, meanwhile, crosses after $9{,}13\,r_s/c$ of proper time and reaches the singularity after $9{,}80$: only $2/3\,r_s/c$ more.

> [Thử ngay] [[Run again from the start|lai]] [[Show everything at once|het]] [[Close-up of the horizon|gan]]
> Drag the green dot on the distant observer’s line to move the “now” sheet up and down yourself. Hover over a yellow dot to read where that flash was sent and when it arrived.
> With sound on: the left ear hears a “tick” each time a flash is sent (by the diagram’s $t^*$), and the right ear hears a note each time the distant observer receives that flash, at a pitch of $660 \times 0{,}6/\Delta t_{\text{obs}}$ Hz, proportional to the received frequency (converted for the ear). The right side grows sparser and lower and then falls silent after flash 16, while the left side keeps ticking up to flash 17.

+++ Going deeper: when each flash arrives
Set $r_s = c = 1$. An outgoing ray obeys $t^* = r + 2\ln|r - 1| + C$. A flash sent at $(t^*_e,\ r_e)$ reaches $r = 7$ at

$$ t^*_{\text{obs}} = t^*_e + (7 - r_e) + 2\ln\frac{6}{r_e - 1} $$

The logarithmic term grows without limit as $r_e \to 1$: each time the astronaut gets $e$ times closer to the horizon, the flash arrives 2 units later. The distant observer is at rest, so their clock runs at $\sqrt{1 - 1/7} \approx 0{,}926$ times $\dd t^*$. The ratio “reception interval / emission interval” is exactly $1 + z$: the light is reddened by that same factor.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Drag the “now” sheet (green dot) to exactly the moment when the distant observer has just received the **last flash**, flash 16 (no more than 1 rs/c late).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: Flash 16 is sent at r ≈ 1.13 rs but reaches r = 7 rs very late, at about t* = 24.3. The data box shows how many flashes have been received.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
The same events, now redrawn with Schwarzschild time $t$ (drag the **Blend coordinates** slider or press a button). The astronaut’s world line shoots up to infinity just before the horizon; the part inside appears as if dropping out of the sky. The cones near the horizon are stretched into threads; the cones inside tip right over sideways.

No event has changed: still 17 flashes, still 16 of them arriving, still reaching the singularity after $9{,}80\,r_s/c$ of proper time. Only the **time labels** stuck on the events are different. The “frozen at the horizon” picture comes from the choice of coordinates.

To find where things truly break down, you need a quantity that does not depend on coordinates. The {{Bất biến Kretschmann|Kretschmann scalar}} measures how strong the curvature is:

$$ K = \frac{12\,r_s^2}{r^6} $$

At the horizon $K = 12/r_s^4$: finite. So $r = r_s$ is only a {{kỳ dị tọa độ|coordinate singularity}}, just as longitude loses its meaning at the North Pole although there is nothing odd about the North Pole. At $r = 0$, $K \to \infty$: that is the true singularity. At $r = 0{,}1\,r_s$, $K$ is already a million times its value at the horizon.

> [Thử ngay] [[Schwarzschild time|schw]] [[Time t*|ef]] [[Stop halfway|giua]]

> [Lưu ý] A thin region next to the horizon ($|r - r_s| \lt 0{,}00002\,r_s$) is cut out when drawing with Schwarzschild time, because $t$ goes to infinity there.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
All the results above are in units of $r_s$ and $r_s/c$. Convert to real black holes using $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ (about 2.95 km per solar mass):

Sgr A* has 4.3 million and M87* 6.5 billion solar masses ($M_\odot$). The radii $r_s$ of the three black holes in the table are 12.7 million km, 128 AU and 29.5 km.

| Black hole ($r_s/c$) | Falling from far: horizon → singularity | Longest |
|---|---|---|
| Sgr A* (42 s) | 28 s | 67 s |
| M87* (17.8 hours) | 12 hours | 28 hours |
| 10 $M_\odot$ (98 µs) | 66 µs | 155 µs |

(µs: microsecond, one millionth of a second.)

Inside the horizon you **cannot stand still**: standing still means keeping $r$ fixed, and $r$ is now time. Just outside you can stand still, but there is a price. The proper acceleration needed to hover at $r_0$ is

$$ a = \frac{c^2}{r_s}\cdot\frac{r_s^2}{2r_0^2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - r_s/r_0}} $$

The last factor goes to infinity at the horizon. At $r_0 = 1{,}01\,r_s$ you need $4{,}93\,c^2/r_s$; for Sgr A* that is about 3.6 million $g$.

> [Tóm lại] Outside the horizon the cones tilt more and more; at the horizon the outer edge stands vertical; inside, the whole cone points toward $r = 0$. The horizon is a surface woven from light; the singularity is a moment. Two coordinate systems, one spacetime.

[[Full view|toan]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: $t$ is Schwarzschild time (a clock very far away). With $t^*$, infalling light is always tilted at 45°.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: No coefficient is infinite at $r = 1$: the coordinates work both inside and outside the horizon.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: Positive outside, 0 at the horizon, negative inside. Infalling light always has $\dd r/\dd t^* = -c$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.ten: Proper time of someone falling from far away
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: From the horizon to the singularity: $\tfrac{2}{3}\,r_s/c$. The longest possible inside: $(\pi/2)\,r_s/c$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Finite at $r = r_s$ (coordinate singularity), infinite at $r = 0$ (true singularity).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: In Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates, what does the outer edge of the light cone look like exactly at the horizon?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: Horizontal: light moves out infinitely fast
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: Vertical: outgoing light stands still at r = rs
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: It vanishes: there is no cone at the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: $\dd r/\dd t^* = c(r - r_s)/(r + r_s) = 0$ at $r = r_s$. A flash of light sent outward from exactly the horizon stays there forever; such rays weave the surface of the horizon. Choosing “it vanishes” confuses this with the picture drawn in Schwarzschild time, where the cone closes up because the coordinates break down.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: An astronaut falls from far away into a black hole of 10 solar masses. By their own clock, how long does it take from crossing the horizon to reaching the singularity?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: $\tau = \tfrac{2}{3}\,r_s/c$ with $r_s = 29{,}5$ km: $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 29\,500 / 299\,792\,458 \approx 6{,}6 \times 10^{-5}$ s. “Forever” is the time by the distant observer’s clock, not the astronaut’s. 28 seconds is the figure for Sgr A*.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Why does a distant observer never see the astronaut cross the horizon?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: Because the astronaut stops before the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: Because light sent closer to the horizon arrives later, and light sent right at the horizon never gets out
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Because the horizon is a wall that blocks light
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: Because tidal forces tear the astronaut apart before the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The arrival time contains the term $2\ln(6/(r_e - 1))$, which grows without limit as $r_e \to r_s$. The astronaut never stops: they cross after a finite proper time. For a large black hole the tidal force at the horizon is very small.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Already inside the horizon, the astronaut fires the rockets at full power, pointing outward. What happens?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: They escape if the rockets are strong enough
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: They manage to stay still at some radius
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: They still reach r = 0, and the proper time left is no longer than in free fall
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Inside, the whole light cone points toward the center, so every world line has $r$ decreasing. Firing the rockets only switches to a different world line inside the cone, and the free-fall line is the one with the longest proper time (at most $(\pi/2)\,r_s/c$).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: In the Schwarzschild metric, the coefficient of dr² is infinite at r = rs. What does that mean?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: The curvature of spacetime is infinite at the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: The Schwarzschild coordinates break down there; the curvature is still finite (K = 12/rs⁴)
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: Space is torn apart at the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.4: Light cannot cross the horizon in either direction
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The Kretschmann scalar $12\,r_s^2/r^6$ does not depend on coordinates and is finite at $r = r_s$. Switch to $t^*$ and every coefficient there is finite. Light crosses the horizon going **in** perfectly normally; it just cannot go **out**.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Explain the statement: “Inside a black hole, the singularity is not a place but a moment.”
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Inside the horizon, the light cone of every event points toward smaller $r$: $r$ decreases along every world line, just as time always increases. So $r = 0$ lies in the **future** of everyone who has gone inside, rather than in some direction in space that you could turn away from. You cannot avoid it any more than you can avoid tomorrow; you can only get there sooner (by firing rockets), or at the latest after $(\pi/2)\,r_s/c$.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 12: Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates, light cones around a black hole, falling into a black hole.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd edition): the observer falling freely from far away (the “rain frame”), inside the horizon.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): the history of the ideas of the horizon and the singularity, told without mathematics.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: C. W. Misner, K. S. Thorne and J. A. Wheeler, *Gravitation* (1973): the parts on Schwarzschild geometry and the coordinate systems that also cover the interior.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A coordinate system for a black hole in which the time $t^* = t + (r_s/c)\ln|r/r_s - 1|$ is tied to infalling light rays. It does not break down at the horizon, so it can draw the interior as well.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: A place where formulas written in one coordinate system give infinity, but the problem disappears when you change coordinates. Examples: $r = r_s$ in the Schwarzschild metric, or longitude at the North Pole.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: The number $R_{abcd}R^{abcd}$, which measures how strong the curvature is and is the same in every coordinate system. Around a Schwarzschild black hole it equals $12\,r_s^2/r^6$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: A surface in spacetime woven from light rays, such as an event horizon. It can be crossed in one direction only.

canh.phat-o-r-rs-luc-dong-ho-phi: Sent at r = {0} rs, when the astronaut’s clock reads τ = {1} rs/c. {2}

canh.hong-duong-the-gioi-nguoi-roi-cham-: Pink: the faller’s world line (white dots: every rs/c of proper time). Yellow: flashes of light. Blue: the distant observer, with the received flashes numbered. The green sheet is “now” by t*: drag the green dot on the distant observer’s line to move it.
canh.truc-dung-la-thoi-gian-san-la-khong: The vertical axis is time, the floor is space around the black hole. Yellow: cones outside the horizon; white: at the horizon; orange-red: inside. The cones are drawn large to be easy to see. Hover over a cone to read its tilt.
